title: The Traffic Cop Your Servers Need
description: Learn why a single server can't handle everything, and how load balancers distribute traffic to keep your system alive.

segments.text: Alright, today we're tackling something you'll see in literally every production system. Load balancing. But let's start from the very beginning — one lonely server doing all the work.
Here's your server. One machine handling every single request. Users come in, it responds. Simple, clean, beautiful. For now.
Now THIS is where it gets interesting. Your app goes viral. Thousands of requests per second flood in. Your poor server is sweating, response times spike, and eventually — it just gives up.
So you've got one overloaded server and a flood of users. What would you do?
segments.thought_prompt: If one server can't handle the load, what's the most obvious solution?

segments.text: You add more servers! But now you have a new problem — who decides which server gets which request? Enter the load balancer. Think of it as a traffic cop standing at the front door, directing every car to the right lane.
The simplest strategy? Round-robin. Request one goes to server A, request two to server B, request three to server C, then back to A. Just take turns. Fair and simple.

But what if server A is twice as powerful as the others? Round-robin wastes that power. Weighted routing sends more traffic to beefier servers. Server A gets two requests for every one the others get.

Here's a crucial piece most beginners miss — health checks. The load balancer constantly pings each server, asking 'Hey, you still alive?' If a server stops responding, it gets pulled from rotation. No more traffic to a dead server.
Let me show you what happens when this breaks. Server B just crashed. Gone.
segments.thought_prompt: What should happen to the requests that were heading to Server B?

segments.text: The load balancer detects the failure through its health check, removes server B from the pool, and redistributes traffic across A and C. Users never even notice. That's the magic — graceful failover.

Every major service you use — Netflix, Google, Amazon — has load balancers sitting in front of thousands of servers. It's the unsung hero of reliability. Without it, one bad server takes down everything.

So remember: load balancers distribute traffic, health checks catch failures, and failover keeps things running. Next up, we'll dive into Layer 4 versus Layer 7 load balancing, and why that distinction matters more than you'd think.
